If the top theme words switched places with the bottom theme words on both sides, this puzzle would be better. If Purgatory had to be included at all (for example, in Catholic theology, no one that goes to Purgatory goes to Hell--everyone in Purgatory eventually goes to Heaven), it makes more sense "above" Hell rather than "below" it. And underworld, well, makes more sense under the revealer. 

On the right side, the name of a waterfall makes more sense at the top since there was a term related to the shoreline (i.e., closer to sea level) which would fit better at the bottom.

A Monday puzzle with some gimmes and some not-so-gimmes, a perfect combination for beginners, and an amusing pastime for old pros.

Am I ignorant or is Tsunami NOT a TIDAL Wave?

The discussion below about "tidal waves" demonstrates a real tension in crosswords, and illustrates how thankless a task writing clues can be.

It is undeniably true that the relationship between tides and tsunamis is tenuous at the very best, but the language is firmly entrenched.  So cluing like "tsunami" is indeed problematic.
But, so would be a clue that cleverly says "Similar to a tsunami, but different" would have been attacked by the every present "Says no one ever".

In other words, using the language as it is typically used is wrong, but so is *not* using language as it is typically used.

@Clancy

No, no, no. Waves that roll in with the tides are called “waves.” Calling out “tidal wave” on a crowded beach would be like calling “fire” in a crowded theater. 

Tsunamis are not caused by the tides, but are sometimes called tidal waves anyway. They were originally called that before the Japanese name was universally adopted. 

Remember, there’s no dog in one, but we still call them hot dogs.

@Clancy - The waves that roll in all the time are not caused by tides. They are caused almost entirely by winds. They are *not* called "tidal waves" and as has already been pointed out, that is as bad a misnomer as calling a tsunami a tidal wave. Frankly, it's worse.
